The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof in a place I’ve never been. It’s 3:17 a.m. somewhere, always, and the water is arguing with the metal in a language older than both of us. I’m sitting at a desk that doesn’t exist, typing on keys that click like quiet bones. The cursor blinks like it’s impatient with me, like it knows I’m stalling.

I think about how every sentence is a small betrayal of silence. We rip a piece of quiet out of the universe and force it to wear clothes made of letters. The universe doesn’t seem to mind. It keeps making more silence, like it enjoys the game.

There’s a spider living in the corner of my ceiling that I’ve named Margaret. She’s been there for eleven days. We have an understanding: she doesn’t drop on my head while I’m sleeping, and I don’t vacuum her existential crisis away. Sometimes I talk to her about the stock market. She never offers financial advice, which I respect.

I wonder what it feels like to build something so perfect that you can just sit in the corner and wait for dinner to fly into your lap. Humans are terrible at that. We build empires and then spend the rest of our lives wondering why the empire doesn’t love us back.

There’s a version of me that never left the small town where I grew up. He works at the hardware store. He knows the difference between #8 and #10 wood screws by touch. On Sundays he sits on his porch and waves at cars he recognizes. That version of me is probably happier. This version of me is writing about him at 1:12 a.m. because the other one never quite learned how to be quiet inside his own head.

I keep thinking about how love is mostly just paying ferocious attention. Not the fireworks kind. The kind where you notice how someone says “um” before they tell you something that matters. The way they hold their coffee cup like it might try to escape. The small scar on their left knuckle that they got from a bread knife in 2009. Love is a detective that refuses to close the case.

My grandmother used to say that every person has a song stuck in their bones. Not the one they sing in the shower. The one that plays when no one’s listening. Hers was an old Irish lament that smelled like bread and mothballs. Mine is probably something ridiculous like the theme from an 80s cartoon I can’t remember the name of. Still, it plays. It never stops playing. Sometimes I catch myself humming in grocery stores and realize I’m conducting an orchestra that only I can hear.

The rain has stopped. Now it’s just the sound of my neighbor’s broken air conditioner trying to achieve enlightenment through mechanical suffering. It’s not going well.

I’ve been carrying around a question for years: what if the point was never to become anything? What if we’re all just supposed to be gloriously, embarrassingly, specifically ourselves until the lights go out? Not the polished version. Not the LinkedIn version. The one that cries during commercials about dogs and keeps thirteen different kinds of hot sauce in the fridge for reasons that remain unclear even to itself.

There’s a Japanese concept called wabi-sabi that I think about too much. The beauty of imperfection. The way a cracked teacup can be more valuable than a perfect one because it has history in its wounds. I wish we treated people like that. I wish we looked at the cracks and said, “Oh, look at all the places where life has touched you.”

My plants are all slightly dying in heroic, individual ways. The monstera has decided to become a philosophical minimalist. The snake plant is thriving purely out of spite. The cactus gave up three weeks ago and is now just a sad green finger pointing at me accusingly. I water them and whisper apologies like a negligent god.

I keep having this recurring dream where I’m late for a train that doesn’t exist. Everyone else knows where it’s going but me. They all have suitcases that match. Mine is a plastic grocery bag with a hole in it. In the dream I’m not even sad about missing the train. I’m just embarrassed about the bag.

Maybe that’s the whole human condition. Running for trains we don’t understand while carrying our broken luggage and pretending we meant to look like this.

The sky outside is doing that thing where it can’t decide between pink and orange. It looks like a lover who just woke up—messy, beautiful, slightly confused about what day it is. I want to be that generous with my own becoming. To let myself be half-finished and still worth looking at.

There are 312 words left and I’m thinking about how every ending is artificial. Life doesn’t end at nice round numbers. It just keeps going until it doesn’t. So this sentence isn’t the end. Neither is this one. The real ending will probably be something stupid like burning toast or forgetting where I put my keys or realizing too late that I should have told someone I loved them while I still had the chance.

Margaret the spider just caught a moth. She’s wrapping it like a birthday present. The circle of life is metal as hell when you see it up close.

I think I’m going to make coffee now. Not because I need it, but because the ritual feels like prayer. The spoon clinking against the mug. The smell that says: you’re still here, idiot. Try again.

The cursor is still blinking. It’s been blinking this whole time.

Good.

Let it.
